title: 2015_PMC4640112_Febrile_seizures_after_2009_influenza_A_H1N1_vaccination_and_inf
ehr_evidence: In addition to information from the national population registry, we used information from the Norwegian Directorate of Health, the Norwegian Surveillance System for Communicable Diseases, the Norwegian Immunisation Register, and the Norwegian Patient Register.
summary: In a nationwide self-controlled case series study of 226,889 Norwegian children born 2006-2009 (up to 45 months of age), the risk of emergency febrile seizures was estimated following 2009 pandemic influenza A (H1N1) vaccination with Pandemrix or influenza infection.
key_findings: The IRR of febrile seizures 1-3 days after vaccination was 2.00 (95% CI: 1.15-3.51), with no increased risk in the 4-7 days after vaccination period.
The IRR of febrile seizures on the same day as a diagnosis of pandemic influenza was 116.70 (95% CI: 62.81-216.90).
A tenfold increased risk was observed 1-3 days after influenza diagnosis (IRR 10.12, 95% CI: 3.82-26.82).
In sensitivity analyses excluding outpatients, the IRR for 1-3 days after vaccination was 2.73 (95% CI: 1.51-4.99) and for the day of influenza diagnosis was 130.2 (95% CI: 64.82-261.30).
Multiple-event Cox proportional-hazards regression gave an HR of 2.01 (95% CI: 1.09-4.42) for 1-3 days after vaccination and 142.84 (95% CI: 76.86-265.46) for the day of influenza diagnosis.
captured_features: ICD-10 codes R56.0 and R56.8 for febrile seizures
ICPC-2 code R80 for influenza-like illness
study_design: Self-controlled case series (SCCS) study using linked national registries
population: 226,889 Norwegian children born January 2006-October 2009, up to 45 months of age, resident in Norway as of October 1st, 2009
exposure_domain: Vaccines (2009 pandemic influenza A H1N1 vaccine Pandemrix) and infectious disease (pandemic influenza infection)
limitations: Limited information on potential confounders available in registry data.
Lack of validity testing of the outcome diagnosis.
Results likely apply to more severe influenza infections, as only 3.6% of children received a primary care influenza diagnosis.
Outcome restricted to emergency episodes, excluding non-emergency health care.
